changes.adapted_text: We construct smooth odd initial data on the three-dimensional torus whose solution of the unforced incompressible Euler equations develops a finite-time singularity. The vorticity magnitude at the stationary particle at the origin tends to infinity, while the velocity converges on the whole torus in every spatial $C^\alpha$ norm with $0<\alpha<5/6$. Away from the origin the velocity and its first time derivative converge locally in every spatial $C^m$ norm. Each new wave has small velocity but a large gradient across its phase planes. The preceding flow amplifies the wave and turns its normal. After the amplitude peaks, the wave number is large enough to leave a strong shear in the orientation needed by the next wave. The launch times accumulate in finite time and the velocity increments are summable. To cancel the phase-averaged error of localization, we choose an initial velocity correction that fixes each particle’s final position to first order. A steep central slope in the wave profile supplies the shear. A shallow return slope bounds the positive pressure curvature in this endpoint problem.

changes.authors_text:
The incompressible Euler equations are among the earliest partial differential equations derived in mathematical physics. Euler presented them in 1755, less than a decade after d’Alembert derived the wave equation for the vibrating string \[[41](#cite-DAlembert1747), [42](#cite-Euler1757)\].

In two dimensions the scalar vorticity is transported, so its $L^\infty$ norm is conserved, and smooth solutions exist for all time \[[45](#cite-Wolibner1933)\]. Yudovich \[[46](#cite-Yudovich1963)\] proved global existence and uniqueness for bounded, possibly nonsmooth initial vorticity. In three dimensions, Fefferman’s description of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Problem stated that the global regularity question was also open for the Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$ and on $\mathbb T^3$ \[[47](#cite-Fefferman2006)\].

changes.authors_text:
The goal of this work is to construct smooth initial data for the incompressible Euler equations on the three-dimensional torus whose solution blows up in finite time. We represent $\mathbb T^3$ by the cube $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ with periodic boundary conditions (opposite faces identified). We write these equations as $$\begin{equation}
 \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p=0,
 \qquad \operatorname{div}u=0
 \quad\hbox{on }\mathbb T^3\times[0,T_*). \tag{1.1}
\end{equation}$$ Local existence and uniqueness for sufficiently regular data go back to Lichtenstein and Günther in the 1920s \[[43](#cite-Lichtenstein1925), [44](#cite-Gunther1926)\]. Classical theory on $\mathbb T^3$ supplies a unique maximal smooth solution from smooth divergence-free data \[[13](#cite-EbinMarsden), [10](#cite-BedrossianVicol)\]. By the Beale–Kato–Majda criterion \[[9](#cite-BKM), [11](#cite-GGPP)\], a smooth solution on $[0,T)$ continues smoothly through $T<\infty$ if $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_{L^\infty}\,\,\mathrm dt<\infty$.

Numerical searches for blow-up include the Taylor–Green vortex study of Morf, Orszag and Frisch \[[48](#cite-MorfOrszagFrisch1980)\] and Kerr’s computations for antiparallel vortex tubes \[[49](#cite-Kerr1993)\]. In a later computation, Hou and Li \[[50](#cite-HouLi2006)\] observed at most double-exponential growth of the maximum vorticity past Kerr’s predicted singular time. Luo and Hou \[[51](#cite-LuoHou2014)\] found numerical evidence for axisymmetric blow-up at the wall of an axially periodic cylinder. Childress, Gilbert and Valiant \[[52](#cite-ChildressGilbertValiant2016)\] studied, analytically and numerically, eroding vortex dipoles in axisymmetric flow without swirl, whose maximal vorticity grows like $t^{4/3}$, and Childress and Gilbert \[[53](#cite-ChildressGilbert2018)\] proposed, by formal asymptotic analysis, the hairpin geometry as a model for finite-time blow-up.

On $\mathbb R^3$, Elgindi \[[15](#cite-ElgindiSingularity)\] constructed finite-time blow-up from $C^{1,\alpha_0}$ initial data for some $\alpha_0>0$. Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi \[[16](#cite-ElgindiGhoulMasmoudi)\] obtained stable, locally self-similar blow-up for finite-energy data in this regularity class. Chen and Hou \[[28](#cite-ChenHouSmoothI), [29](#cite-ChenHouSmoothII)\] prove nearly self-similar blow-up from smooth axisymmetric data in a periodic cylinder with boundary, using computer-assisted estimates. The theorem below concerns smooth periodic data on $\mathbb T^3$, with bounded velocity and vorticity growth concentrated at the origin.

changes.adapted_text: *One wave and its successor.* At the origin oddness gives $u(t,0)=0$. Taking the curl of (1.1) there gives $\partial_t\omega(t,0)=(\nabla u(t,0))\omega(t,0)$. A wave can change this gradient substantially while adding little velocity. If its velocity is $\mathbf a F(k\cdot x)$ with $F'(0)=1$ and $\mathbf a\perp k$, its gradient at the origin is $\mathbf a\otimes k$ and its curl is $k\times\mathbf a$. Shortening the wavelength increases the gradient at a fixed amplitude. The rank-one gradient annihilates its own curl. Its role in the construction is to act on a *different* wave.

changes.adapted_text: The wave equations along one particle determine neither a divergence-free velocity near it nor the pressure throughout the torus. We localize the wave, then correct the resulting error. For its average over one period of the phase we select the initial velocity correction by fixing the particles’ end positions to first order. This choice changes the initial data even for waves that start later. The remaining errors can be made small enough to repeat the step. The launch intervals have finite total length, and the velocity increments are summable. On each interval between launches, projection onto the newest normal eliminates the newest leading curl and detects the preceding one. This gives vorticity divergence throughout the approach to the singular time.
changes.authors_text: At each step in the sequence we add an oscillation at a higher frequency, localized near the origin and initially small in velocity. The velocity gradient of the preceding scales amplifies the new oscillation, whose gradient in turn drives the growth of the next one. The growth intervals have finite total length. This multiscale construction follows the approach of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa for the Euler equations with forcing and for forced IPM \[[18](#cite-CMZForcedEuler), [19](#cite-CMZForcedIPM)\]. Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa and Zheng \[[17](#cite-CMZUnforcedEuler)\] used a cascade of vorticity layers to obtain blow-up for the unforced Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$ from $C^{1,\alpha}$ data smooth away from the origin. Related constructions give blow-up with forcing for the inviscid Boussinesq equations, the variable-density Euler equations and the hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations \[[20](#cite-CLMZForcedBoussinesq), [21](#cite-CLMZNonhomogeneousEuler), [22](#cite-CMZHypodissipativeNS)\]. Our companion papers proving singularity formation for forced IPM, the forced Boussinesq equations, and the forced Euler equations \[[3](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterCoiculescuIPM), [1](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterBoussinesq), [2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler)\] use forces smooth in space and time up to the singular time. In the present construction we use Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks and choose the initial velocity at each step so that the limiting solution is unforced.

changes.adapted_text: *The velocity at the singular time.* The convergence in $C^\alpha(\mathbb T^3)$ for $0<\alpha<5/6$ is derived in Section 8.4 from the sizes of the velocity increments and their first derivatives. Jaswal obtains the same convergence \[[57](#cite-JaswalTerminal), Theorem 1.5(a)\]. The bounds between launches also give $\int_0^{T_*}|\omega(t,0)|\,\,\mathrm dt=\infty$ at the fixed particle. For comparison, the global integrals in (1.2) already follow from finite maximal lifespan by the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda criterion \[[9](#cite-BKM), p. 62, Theorem and Corollary\]\[[11](#cite-GGPP), Theorem 1\].
changes.authors_text: Convex integration constructions of nonunique weak solutions of the Euler equations also use oscillations at successive frequency scales. Below the Onsager exponent, this method yields solutions with nonconstant kinetic energy \[[23](#cite-IsettOnsager), [6](#cite-BDLSVOnsager)\]. For the unforced Euler equations in the plane, Coiculescu \[[24](#cite-CoiculescuEulerI), [25](#cite-CoiculescuEulerII)\] uses nested vortex rings at different scales. An instability propagates from the inner rings outward, yielding distinct renormalized weak solutions with the same initial vorticity. See also Choi \[[26](#cite-ChoiEulerNonuniqueness)\] and Hou, Qin, Song and Zhang \[[27](#cite-HouQinSongZhangEulerNonuniqueness)\]. For the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations, Jia and Šverák \[[54](#cite-JiaSverak2015)\] gave a conditional construction of nonunique Leray–Hopf solutions based on spectral assumptions about forward self-similar flows. Nonuniqueness was shown for finite-energy weak solutions by Buckmaster and Vicol \[[7](#cite-BuckmasterVicolNS)\], and in the Leray–Hopf class with a common force by Albritton, Brué and Colombo \[[4](#cite-AlbrittonBrueColombo)\]. In a recent preprint, Buckmaster, Coiculescu and Li \[[8](#cite-BuckmasterCoiculescuLiNS)\] obtain nonuniqueness of unforced Leray–Hopf solutions.

*Turning.* Suppose for a moment that $\eta=0$. Then $E_3$ and $k=\lambda E_3$ stay fixed and the two-component system above admits exponential growth. Yet $D\mathbf a$ stays in the $(E_1,E_2)$-plane, so $k\cdot D\mathbf a=0$. The growing wave supplies no first coupling for a successor. With $\eta>0$ the normal develops a component towards $-E_2$ in the moving frame, which the shear turns towards $E_1$. Measure elapsed time in units of the growth time by putting $\tau=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}\,t$. As $S\to\infty$ with $\varepsilon$ and the normalized time interval fixed, the components of $k/\lambda$ in the preceding frame tend to $(\tan\varphi,0,1)$, where $$\tan\varphi=\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau^2,\qquad 0\le\varphi<\tfrac\pi2.$$ Thus $\varphi$ is the angle from $E_3$ towards $E_1$ of the limiting normal. At finite shear the actual projected normal has slope $(k\cdot E_1)/(k\cdot E_3)$, which the comparison estimate in Section 2 controls.

Turning changes the pressure force in the amplitude equation. The coefficient $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)$ that drives the initial growth changes sign at $\tau=\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. The $E_2$ component of the reference amplitude, denoted $a_{\rm ref}$ and equal to one at launch, continues to grow. It reaches its maximum when its logarithmic derivative vanishes, at a time $\tau_m$ with $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$ (Lemma 2.5). Figure 1 shows this delay. To transfer the gain to a wave at finite shear, Section 2 measures its amplitude relative to $a_{\rm ref}$. Under the comparison hypotheses on an interval containing $\tau_m$, its maximum is at least a fixed multiple of $\exp(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$ times its launch value (Lemma 2.6 and Proposition 2.8).

changes.adapted_text:
*Transfer to the successor.* The present wave will supply the shear and its parent matrix $D$ will play the role now held by $B$. We therefore measure $D$ in the present wave’s frame. $$E_{1,+}=k/|k|,\quad E_{2,+}=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|,\quad
 E_{3,+}=E_{1,+}\times E_{2,+},\qquad
 \nu_+=E_{1,+}\cdot D E_{2,+},\quad
 \eta_+=E_{3,+}\cdot D E_{2,+}.$$ At launch the small $-S^{-1}E_1$ component in the amplitude reverses the sign of $\eta_+$. With zero tilt one gets $-\nu$. With the chosen tilt one gets $(-\nu+\sigma S^{-2})/(1+S^{-2})>0$, since $\sigma=2\nu S^2$. A vanishing tilt can thus determine whether another amplification is possible.

Prescribe a smaller ratio $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ for the successor. We can launch it as soon as $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$ in the interval specified below. First, $\nu_+$ stays positive throughout amplification, which gives the pressure coefficient $p_{\rm w}=2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$ its sign. At late times $\nu_+$ is close to $\nu$ and $\eta_+/\nu_+$ is comparable to $\cos\varphi$ (Lemma 2.7). Under the hypotheses of Proposition 2.8 the ratio is still above its target at the reference peak and below it at $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$. Continuity gives a crossing after the reference peak. There the increased normal length offsets the decrease relative to the maximal amplitude $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ on the comparison interval. $$\frac{|\mathbf a|}{A}\asymp\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon_+}{\varepsilon}},
 \qquad |k|\asymp\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_+},\qquad
 |\mathbf a|\,|k|\asymp
          \frac{\lambda A}{\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}} .$$ Here $\asymp$ allows absolute constant factors. The product in the last estimate is the shear available to the successor.

For the reference solution one can see directly why the amplitude peak is too early to judge the shear. Its normal has length $\lambda\sec\varphi$. From (2.14), $$a_{\rm ref}\,\sec\varphi
 =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos\varphi}}\,
   \exp\!\left(\int_0^\tau(1+e)\cos\varphi\,\,\mathrm d\tau'\right).$$ Here $e\ge0$ and $\varphi$ increases, so the reference shear continues to increase after $a_{\rm ref}$ peaks. For the finite-shear wave we use the bounds at a crossing in Proposition 2.8.

changes.adapted_text:
To transfer the affine calculation to the torus, localize the wave near the origin. Give each particle its phase and its cutoff value at time zero, then transport them by the flow of the preceding periodic velocity. The cutoff vanishes near the faces of a fundamental cell in the particle labels. Hence the wave extends smoothly across opposite faces even when its initial normal has nonintegral components. Transport of phase along a given flow also occurs in the short-wave stability equations of Lifschitz and Hameiri \[[37](#cite-LifschitzHameiri1991), §II, (7), (9), (17)\] and of Friedlander and Vishik \[[38](#cite-FriedlanderVishik1991), (5)–(7)\]. The broader asymptotic-wave theory goes back to Lax \[[39](#cite-Lax1957)\] and Choquet-Bruhat \[[40](#cite-ChoquetBruhat1969), §§2–3, pp. 3–6\]. Le Dizès and Leblanc \[[58](#cite-LeDizesLeBlanc2006), §2\] identified a difficulty with iterating plane waves over a general base flow. The equations for a wave along one trajectory do not give a global solution when its coefficients depend on the particle label unless the extra spatial derivative terms also cancel. Here we differentiate the amplitude, transported phase and cutoff across labels and correct the resulting divergence and momentum errors.

For the starting shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, let $e_i$ be the coordinate vectors and take $\rho>0$ small. In the initial frame of the first constructed wave, whose normal points along $e_1$ and whose amplitude points along $e_2$, the gradient $\nabla U_0(0)$ has $\nu=2\pi$ and $\eta=2\pi\rho$. Section 6 uses this first wave to start the successive amplifications.

Throughout one correction step we keep the parent $U$ fixed. Its Fourier support is bounded, so Bernstein’s inequality controls its higher derivatives. Its residual $R_U$ includes the error from the preceding truncation.

For the flow $X$ of $U$ from time zero, assign each particle label $a$ in the fundamental cell a phase $k_*\cdot a$, with $k_*\ne0$. Thus $$\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a,\qquad \kappa=\nabla_x\theta.$$ The particle keeps its phase, but the phase surfaces deform and their normal $\kappa$ changes. For a wave after the first, $k_*$ is chosen so that $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ at the origin at launch. To describe the velocity, first keep the phase $s$ independent in a periodic profile $A_1(t,x,s)$ and then put $s=\theta(t,x)$. A spatial derivative of the evaluated profile differentiates both $x$ at fixed $s$ and the phase, with factor $\kappa$. A smooth time cutoff $\widetilde\chi$ switches on each later wave during the first part of its amplification interval. The first wave is present at time zero and uses $\widetilde\chi=1$.
changes.authors_text:
We smoothly truncate the velocity of each step in frequency at the end of the step, to simplify the bookkeeping of derivative estimates, as in the mollification step of convex integration \[[6](#cite-BDLSVOnsager), Section 2.4\]. This introduces a small error, carried to the next step; Subsection 5.7 gives the estimates. Write $U$ for the truncated velocity of the preceding step and $R_U$ for its residual in the Euler equations.

We add the localized wave described in Subsection 1.1, using $F_h$ and a divergence correction. Let $X$ be the flow of $U$ from time zero, and fix a nonzero vector $k_*$. The phase $\theta$ of the localized wave is defined by $$\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$$ for Lagrangian coordinates $a$ in the fundamental cell. It is the plane phase $k_*\cdot x$ at time zero, transported by $U$. Its gradient $\kappa=\nabla_x\theta$ is the wave vector of the localized wave; for a linear flow, $\theta=\kappa\cdot x$, as in Subsection 1.1. For a wave after the first, $k_*$ is chosen so that $\kappa=\lambda E_3$ at the origin at its activation time, as for the new wave of Subsection 1.1. The leading velocity is $A_1(t,x,\theta(t,x))$. Writing the profile as $A_1(t,x,s)$ with $s$ independent lets us distinguish derivatives of the coefficients from the large term $\kappa\partial_s$ that arises when differentiating through the phase. A wave after the first is multiplied by a cutoff $\widetilde\chi(t)$ in time that vanishes before its amplification interval; for the first wave $\widetilde\chi=1$. The derivative of the cutoff leaves an error of the size of the wave at the start of that interval, also carried to the next step.

The mean correction $B_2$ cancels the phase average of $H_2$ together with the parent residual. With $D_t=\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x$, the linearized Euler equation (1.6) gives $D_t B_2+(\nabla U)B_2+\nabla q=-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U$ with $\operatorname{div}B_2=0$. The Jacobi inverse selects $B_2(0)$ so that the correction leaves the truncated parent’s final particle positions fixed to first order.

changes.adapted_text:
The forced Boussinesq construction of Alpöge and Buckmaster \[[1](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterBoussinesq), Section 1.2\] uses a force to rotate the temperature gradient and the wave direction together. This preserves their amplifying coupling while changing the horizontal wave number and the sign of vorticity production. A shooting parameter returns the horizontal wave number and the vorticity amplitude to zero. The temperature gradient retains its gain, and a successor grows while the predecessor’s wave vector stays vertical.

For forced axisymmetric Euler with swirl \[[2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler), Section 1.2\], circulation replaces temperature and couples to azimuthal vorticity. Angular control returns the central azimuthal-vorticity amplitude to zero. Radial coefficients require amplitudes that vary across the transported support. In both forced constructions a smooth force also absorbs the final error. The Boussinesq layers even remain exactly linear on a neighborhood of their successors, where the streamfunction corrections vanish. Here incompressibility determines the wave pressure and the wave equations supply the turn. We retain the gradient at the central particle, estimate its variation across the next wave, and send the residual to zero.

The successive scales owe much to Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s constructions for forced Euler \[[18](#cite-CMZForcedEuler), Section 1.2\] and the forced incompressible porous media equation \[[19](#cite-CMZForcedIPM), Sections 1.2.1–1.2.4\]. With smooth space-time forcing the latter construction is developed in \[[3](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterCoiculescuIPM), Theorem 2.1\]. Córdoba, Martínez-Zoroa and Zheng \[[17](#cite-CMZUnforcedEuler), Theorem 2\] used layers of vorticity on $\mathbb R^3$ for unforced Euler with $C^{1,\alpha}$ initial data smooth away from the origin. For blow-up with forcing in Boussinesq, variable-density Euler and hypodissipative Navier–Stokes, see \[[20](#cite-CLMZForcedBoussinesq), Theorem 1\], \[[21](#cite-CLMZNonhomogeneousEuler), Theorem 1\] and \[[22](#cite-CMZHypodissipativeNS), Theorem 1\].

changes.authors_text:
The construction of blow-up for the forced Boussinesq equations by Alpöge and Buckmaster \[[1](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterBoussinesq), Section 1.2\] also uses coupled wave amplitudes to amplify a gradient and prepare the next wave. There the temperature gradient grows together with a vorticity amplitude. The accompanying shear would obstruct the next growth stage, so an external force rotates the temperature gradient and wave direction together. This preserves the coupling that drives the temperature amplitude while changing the horizontal component of the wave vector, and hence the sign of vorticity production. A scalar shooting parameter selects a rotation pulse that returns the vorticity amplitude and that horizontal component to zero, retaining the temperature gain. Keeping the wave vector vertical then holds both amplitudes fixed while the next wave grows.

The construction of blow-up for the forced Euler equations by Alpöge and Buckmaster \[[2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler), Section 1.2\] builds on this mechanism for axisymmetric flow with swirl. Circulation replaces temperature and couples to azimuthal vorticity. The angular control returns the principal azimuthal-vorticity amplitude at the material center to zero while retaining the circulation-gradient gain. The radial dependence of the elliptic operator and of this coupling requires amplitudes that vary across the transported support, with transport by the preceding velocity, including its corrections.

Localization presents a further difference. In the construction for the Boussinesq equations the profiles are linear near zero, so each layer’s velocity and temperature are exactly linear on a region containing the later layers. The streamfunction corrections vanish there, preserving this region. In both forced constructions, the remaining errors are absorbed by a force smooth through the singular time. To solve the unforced Euler equations, we must remove those errors. The pressure and velocity corrections need not preserve a neighborhood on which the velocity is linear; the next wave uses the central gradient and estimates on its spatial variation.

changes.adapted_text:
The calculation has three uses. An exact wave in a linear Euler flow gives equations for its normal and amplitude. Those equations still make sense for a prescribed matrix, and we shall solve a strong-shear reference problem in the moving frame of a preceding wave. Finally, a quantitative comparison will transfer its growth, pressure sign and successor geometry to the central gradient of the periodic construction.

Begin with a linear velocity $Dx$ on $\mathbb R^3$. If $D(t)$ is smooth and trace free, with $D'+D^2$ symmetric, the background $Dx$ has pressure $-x\cdot(D'+D^2)x/2$. Choose a smooth odd $1$-periodic profile $F$ with $F'(0)=1$. Oddness gives $F$ zero phase mean, so it has a periodic primitive $P$. Choose its additive constant so that $\langle P\rangle_s=0$, where $\langle H\rangle_s=\int_0^1 H(s)\,\,\mathrm ds$.

changes.adapted_text:
A large velocity gradient is useful a second time only if the wave which created it can amplify a successor. The frame of the preceding wave distinguishes two entries of the older gradient, $\nu=E_1\cdot
BE_2$ and $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$. The first sets the growth rate together with the shear strength $\sigma$. The second rotates the normal out of its launch direction. Their ratio fixes the normalized time available before the reference amplitude peaks. Both couplings must then be estimated in the *new* frame, where their ratio determines the next launch.

We first solve the wave equations with these two entries held constant in the preceding wave’s moving frame and pass to the strong-shear limit (Lemma 2.3). We then compare the actual coefficients and amplitudes with this reference system on a prescribed interval. Dividing out the growing reference amplitude in (2.15) lets us control the wave’s direction. Near the successor’s launch $\eta_+/\nu_+$ is small. Lemma 2.7 compares it with $\cos\varphi$ to relative accuracy, enough to locate a crossing even when the target ratio tends to zero. Proposition 2.8 bounds the shear at that crossing and the amplitude in the first unit of normalized time. The wave is small while its time cutoff changes, so activation produces little error. At the later crossing the product of its amplitude and its wave number is large, so the next wave can grow.

Fix the time-zero wave vector $k_*\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and give the particle with label $a$ the phase $\phi(a)=k_*\cdot a$. The transported phase $\phi\circ X(t,\cdot)^{-1}$ has Eulerian gradient $\kappa=\mathbf d\phi=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ at $X(t,a)$. For a flow linear in $a$ the transported phase is $\kappa\cdot x$, as in Lemma 2.1. A profile $f(t,a,s)$ has two spatial arguments: the initial particle position $a$ and an independent periodic phase $s\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, measured in cycles. Its value in the fluid is obtained by setting $s=\phi(a)$ and $x=X(t,a)$. Denote the resulting field by $f^\natural$: $$f^\natural(t,X(t,a))=f(t,a,\phi(a)),\qquad
 \widetilde{\mathbf d}=\mathbf d+\kappa\partial_s .$$ For example, the profile called $A_1(t,x,s)$ in the introduction is written here as $A_1(t,X(t,a),s)$ when pulled back to the labels. This substitution still leaves $s$ free. Evaluation at $s=k_*\cdot a$ is a separate operation.

Before evaluation $\mathbf d$ is the Eulerian spatial derivative at fixed phase, written in labels. After evaluation a change of position also changes the phase by its gradient $\kappa$, which gives the additional derivative $\kappa\partial_s$. Time differentiation along $X$ keeps both $a$ and its phase fixed. Thus

$$\begin{equation}
 \nabla_x f^\natural=(\widetilde{\mathbf d}f)^\natural,\qquad
 (\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla_x)f^\natural=(f_t)^\natural. \tag{3.1}
\end{equation}$$ The phase modulo one is periodic in $a$ exactly when $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$. To allow arbitrary $k_*$, we evaluate the oscillatory profiles on the lifted label cell $[-1/2,1/2]^3$ and extend periodically. They vanish near the cell boundary, so the extension is smooth. Phase-independent profiles are already periodic in $a$.

*Time integral along the central particle.* The interval estimates give $\int_0^{T_*}|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\,\,\mathrm dt=\infty$ by bounding both the vorticity and the duration of each interval. On a sufficiently late interval $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, let $r$ be the rate of wave $j$. The crossing occurs at normalized time $r(t_{j+1}-t_j)\ge\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon_{j-1}=2L_j^2$. Multiplication yields $$\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\,\,\mathrm dt\ge cL_j

The authors describe the origins of their argument as follows.

Before OpenAI released its paper on the unforced Euler equations, the first and second authors had completed a second proof of blow-up for the Euler equations with smooth forcing. Unlike their public proof \[[2](#cite-AlpogeBuckmasterForcedEuler)\], which uses axisymmetric flow with swirl, this unreleased proof uses the same Craik–Criminale amplification mechanism as OpenAI’s paper, including the same reduced equations for the amplitude of a wave, the system (2.5) above. In our unpublished work on the hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations, much of the argument for removing the force was developed, with human prompts guiding that work. This is consistent with the second author’s statement of September 7 that the hypodissipative work pointed toward a blow-up construction for the unforced Euler equations \[[30](#cite-BuckmasterSeptemberStatement)\].

The second author’s account of his communications with OpenAI about these results is given in \[[30](#cite-BuckmasterSeptemberStatement)\].

The following is the authors’ account of how they wrote their source manuscript.

We used Claude and Codex throughout this work. The first proof without force was written by Anthropic models from the drafts on the Euler equations with forcing and on the hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations described above. Like the first writeups of our proofs for the Boussinesq and Euler equations, it was long and hard to read. We then rewrote it with Claude and Codex under our direction, iterating with the models on the structure of the argument, isolating the key ideas, and simplifying it over successive revisions. In the course of this we replaced parts of the argument by ideas of our own, which the models implemented. Together with our own editing, this led to the present text.

changes.adapted_text: At every fixed time order $q\ge1$ the induction over levels $p\ge2$ of (M.5.40) has the form $$\mathcal J_{q,n,\gamma}(f_p+f_p^S)+\lambda^{1/2}\mathcal J_{q,n}(B_p) \le C_{n,p,q}\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}\qquad(n\ge0).$$ To see how the parent factors disappear, take $p=2$. The averaged stress and (2.2) bound $\mathcal J_{q-1,n+1}(\bar f_2)$ by $C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/2}$. The mean inverse (2.3) thus gives $\lambda^{1/2}\mathcal J_{q,n}(B_2)\le C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-2}$, where we have enlarged $a_q$. The three contributions to $f_2$ in (M.5.25) have respective powers $\lambda^{-9/4}$, $\lambda^{-5/2}$ and $\lambda^{-2}$. Their largest power is $\lambda^{-2}=\lambda^{-23/12}\lambda^{-1/12}$. The same spare $\lambda^{-1/12}$ occurs in the bound for the mean. Once it has absorbed the parent factor in that bound, the term $f_2^S=-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s V_1$ has a further margin $\lambda^{-1/4}$ relative to $\lambda^{-23/12}$. The same margins recur at every level. The lower levels satisfy the displayed induction bound at every spatial order with no power of $\mu$. We estimate $\bar f_p$ at time order $q-1$ and one higher spatial order, then apply (2.3) before using $B_p$ in $f_p^S$. Each term uses a bounded number of the coefficient, product and inverse estimates, so their combined factor is $C_q\mu^{a_q}$ with $a_q$ independent of $p$ and $P$. The additional source $f_p^S$ has the margin $\lambda^{-1/4}$ from the proof of Theorem M.5.6. Even the smallest margin, $\lambda^{-1/12}$, absorbs the parent power for large $j$ since $\lambda=\mu^{K_j}$ and $K_j\to\infty$. Dependence on $n,p,q$ remains in $C_{n,p,q}$. This proves the induction bound and (M.5.34)–(M.5.36) in the time norms, with $C_q\mu^{a_q}$ in place of $\mathsf D^C$. The mean pressures do not enter this induction. Summing to depth $P$ as in Theorem M.5.6 gives the respective bounds $C_{n,P,q}\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/4}$ for the weighted norm of $W_{\rm osc}$, $C_{n,P,q}\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/2}$ for the unweighted mean sum $\bar W$, and $C_{n,P,q}\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$ for the unweighted remainder $R_P$. The weighted norm of $R_{\widetilde\chi}$ is bounded by $C_q\mu^{a_q}\lambda^{-5/4}$. It and all its time derivatives vanish outside $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$.

The proof uses the hypothesis $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$ of the theorem only to absorb powers of $\mathsf D$. changes.authors_text: *Proof of Theorem 1.1.* By Theorem M.7.1, on $[0,S_j]$ the oscillation $O_j$ is supported in the ball of radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$ about the origin, and these radii tend to zero. Fix a compact set $K\subset\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$. Only finitely many $O_j$ meet a neighborhood of $K$. For every fixed pair $(m,q)$, (1.2) and $\sum_j\lambda_j^{-1}<\infty$ give a summable bound for the remaining increments in $C^q([0,T_\infty];C^m(K))$. The finitely many earlier terms are smooth there because $S_j>T_\infty$. The sum therefore converges with every mixed derivative up to $T_\infty$ away from zero. Its limit equals $u$ before $T_\infty$ by Proposition M.8.1.
